title: Realizing a solvable subgroup as a flag stabilizer
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type, and all subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness, connectedness and morphism properties have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-pc-morphism-conventions]. A group is solvable if its successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroups eventually become trivial. Let $G$ be smooth and connected and let $H\subseteq G$ be smooth, connected and solvable. There exist a nonzero finite-dimensional $F$-vector space $V$, a faithful group-scheme representation $r:G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ (a closed immersion), and a complete flag $\mathcal F:0=V_0\subset V_1\subset\cdots\subset V_n=V$, $\dim V_i=i$, whose scheme-theoretic stabilizer in $G$ is exactly $H$. The functor $\operatorname{Fl}(V)$ of complete flags of locally direct-summand submodules of $V\otimes_F A$ is represented by a projective finite-type $F$-scheme; in particular every closed reduced subscheme of it is proper and of finite type over $F$. For any faithful representation of $G$ on a finite-dimensional vector space and any complete flag $\mathcal E$, let $K$ be its scheme-theoretic stabilizer. Then $K_{\mathrm{red}}^\circ$, the identity component of the reduced subgroup scheme, is smooth, connected and solvable and has $\dim K_{\mathrm{red}}^\circ=\dim K$.

source.place: Theorems 4.9 and 4.27, pp.87,94--95 (add a faithful representation to the line-stabilizer representation before forming the flag); Theorem 16.30, pp.334--335, applied to H on V/V_1 in the proof of Theorem 17.9, p.354; Propositions 7.29--7.30, pp.146--147; reduced identity subgroup over a perfect field, Section 1 (1.39), and solvable triangular subgroups, Section 16a.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-chevalley-scheme-line-stabilizer] to $H\subseteq G$, obtaining a rational representation $E$ and a line $L\subseteq E$ with stabilizer $H$ on every $F$-algebra. For a faithful representation, apply [lem-sfb-normal-subgroup-representation-kernel] with the trivial normal subgroup of $G$. Its homomorphism $s:G\to\operatorname{GL}(W)$ has trivial scheme-theoretic kernel. By [lem-sfb-algebraic-group-homomorphism-factorization], its closed image is the fppf sheaf quotient by that kernel, hence is $G$ itself. Therefore $s$ is a closed immersion, with $\dim W\geq1$.

source.place: Theorem 4.27, pp.94–95; Theorem 4.9, p.87; closed faithful representation via the existing prescribed-kernel and homomorphism theorems.

proof.text: Put $V=E\oplus W$ with the direct-sum representation $r=\rho\oplus s$, and regard $L$ as $L\oplus0$. Its stabilizer remains $H$ on every algebra, since $g(L\oplus0)=L\oplus0$ if and only if $\rho(g)L=L$. The block-diagonal inclusion $\operatorname{GL}(E)\times\operatorname{GL}(W)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}(V)$ is closed: set the off-diagonal entries to zero; invertibility of the full determinant makes both block determinants units. The graph of $\rho$ over the closed copy $s(G)$ is closed, since in affine coordinates it is defined by equating each first-block matrix entry and inverse determinant to the corresponding regular function on $s(G)$. Thus $r$ is a closed immersion. In particular $V\ne0$.

source.place: Theorem 17.9, p.354, first paragraph, with the faithful direct-summand refinement justified by the displayed block equations.

proof.text: Induct on $d=\dim M$ to construct an $H$-stable complete flag in every rational $H$-module $M$, $\sigma:H\to\operatorname{GL}(M)$. At $d=0$ use the empty flag. At $d>0$, let $Y=G_F(d,d-1)$ from [lem-sfb-free-quotient-grassmann-projective]; its $T$-points are rank-$(d-1)$ quotients of $M\otimes_F\mathcal O_T$, equivalently their kernels, the rank-one locally direct summands (a locally free quotient splits locally, and the summand determines its quotient). The rule $(h,S)\mapsto\sigma_T(h)S$ is natural in $T$ and satisfies the action identities, so by representability it is an action $H\times_FY\to Y$. For $d=1$, $Y=\operatorname{Spec}F$; for $d\geq2$, $Y$ has the Plücker closed immersion into $\mathbf P^{d-1}_F$, and is quasi-compact. Hence $Y$ is projective, proper by [lem-pc-projective-proper], of finite type by [def-weil-proper-morphism], and nonempty since $M$ has a line. [lem-sfb-solvable-proper-fixed-point] gives $y\in Y(F)$ fixed by $H$: $y$ is a line $D\subseteq M$, $y_A$ is $D\otimes_FA$, so $\sigma_A(h)(D\otimes_FA)=D\otimes_FA$ for all $A$ and $h\in H(A)$. In a basis beginning with $D$, the lower-left block of the action is zero, so the lower-right block gives a rational action on $M/D$. The inductive flag there pulls back, preceded by $0\subset D$, to a complete flag in $M$, stable over every algebra. Apply this construction to the rational $H$-module $V/L$. Taking inverse images in $V$ gives a complete flag $\mathcal F$ with $V_1=L$. Every $H(A)$ preserves it; conversely its stabilizer preserves $L_A$ and therefore belongs to $H(A)$ by step 1. The equality is natural in $A$, proving equality of subgroup schemes.

source.place: Corollary 17.3 (Borel fixed point) and Theorem 17.4 (Lie–Kolchin via 17.3), p.353; Theorem 17.9, p.354, first paragraph.

proof.text: For $n=\dim V$, [lem-sfb-free-quotient-grassmann-projective] represents rank-$i$ subbundles of $V$ by $X_i=G_F(n,n-i)$ with universal kernel $S_i$ and quotient $Q_i$. Indeed a locally free quotient has a locally split surjection, so its kernel is a locally direct summand; conversely such a summand determines its quotient. Work on $P=\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}X_i$; if $n=1$, put $P=\operatorname{Spec}F$. Impose, for $1\leq i<n-1$, that the composite $S_i\to V\otimes_F\mathcal O_P\to Q_{i+1}$ vanish. In local frames its finitely many matrix entries generate an ideal; frame changes multiply by invertible matrices, so these ideals agree on overlaps and define a closed subscheme $Z\subseteq P$. For every test scheme $T$, a map $T\to P$ factors through $Z$ exactly when all these pulled-back entries vanish, namely $S_i|_T\subseteq S_{i+1}|_T$. The resulting filtration has locally free successive quotients: locally split $V/S_i\twoheadrightarrow V/S_{i+1}$; its kernel is $S_{i+1}/S_i$. Adding $0$ and $V_T$ therefore identifies $Z$ with the stated full-flag functor, naturally under all base changes, including nonreduced test algebras.

source.place: Propositions 7.29–7.30, pp.146–147: Grassmannian incidence construction, written on arbitrary test schemes; quotient Grassmannians: Stacks Tag 089T, constructions.tex, lemma-gkn-representable.

proof.text: Each $X_i$ has a Plücker closed immersion into a finite projective space by [lem-sfb-free-quotient-grassmann-projective]. Repeated [lem-chow-segre] embeds the finite product $P$ into a single projective space. The product of the closed immersions is closed (on affine charts its ideal is the sum of the pulled-back ideals), and composing with $Z\hookrightarrow P$ is closed (successive quotient ring maps are surjective). For $n=1$ use $\operatorname{Spec}F=\mathbf P^0_F$. Hence $Z=\operatorname{Fl}(V)$ is projective; it is quasi-compact as a closed subscheme of $\mathbf P^N_F$. Every closed subscheme $C\subseteq Z$, including every closed reduced one, has the same kind of closed embedding by composition. By [lem-pc-projective-proper] both $Z$ and $C$ are proper over $F$; by [def-weil-proper-morphism] properness includes finite type. This proves all the geometric clauses.

source.place: Proposition 7.30, p.147; Stacks constructions.tex, Tag 01WD, lemma-segre-embedding; morphisms.tex, Tag 01WC, lemma-locally-projective-proper.

proof.text: Now take any faithful representation and complete flag $\mathcal E$ on a space of dimension $m$. For $m=0$, faithfulness forces $G=1$, so all remaining assertions are immediate. For $m>0$ choose an adapted basis. The subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}_m$ preserving this flag is $B_m$, defined on every algebra by setting all entries below the diagonal to zero. Thus $K=G\times_{\operatorname{GL}_m}B_m$ is an affine closed subgroup of finite type; its defining equations are the pullbacks of those entries. By [lem-sfb-locally-algebraic-group-identity-component], $J=(K^0)_{\mathrm{red}}$ is a smooth connected closed subgroup with the same topological space as $K^0$. It equals $(K_{\mathrm{red}})^0$: reduction does not change the topological space, and restriction to the open and closed identity component commutes with quotienting by the nilradical. This is the requested $K_{\mathrm{red}}^\circ$, and $J\subseteq B_m$.

source.place: Section 1, Corollary 1.39, pp.18–19; Theorem 17.9, p.354, stabilizers paragraph, with reduction before taking the smooth identity subgroup; Stacks groupoids.tex, Tags 0B7R,047R,047P,047N.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-triangular-diagonal-kernel] to the smooth connected subgroup $J\subseteq B_m$. It gives a smooth unipotent normal subgroup $U$ and a quotient $J/U$ embedded into $(\mathbf G_m)^m$, hence commutative. By [lem-sfb-smooth-unipotent-solvable], $U$ has a terminating closed normal series with commutative quotients. Prepend $J\supseteq U$ to that series. If its terms are $J=J_0\supseteq J_1\supseteq\cdots\supseteq J_t=1$, the commutator morphism of each $J_i$ is trivial in its commutative quotient, so $\mathcal D(J_i)\subseteq J_{i+1}$. Monotonicity of commutator subgroups then gives $\mathcal D^i(J)\subseteq J_i$ by induction, and $\mathcal D^t(J)=1$. This is solvability in the item\'s convention.

source.place: Section 16a, Proposition 16.2(c)⇒(d), p.325, and Proposition 14.21, pp.284–285; pass explicitly from a solvable normal series to the derived series.

proof.text: Finally [lem-sfb-group-neutral-component-translates] gives finitely many connected components of $K$, each isomorphic to $K^0$ by a translation. An irreducible closed chain lies in a single component of a finite clopen partition; consequently the topological Krull dimension of $K$ is the maximum of the dimensions of its components, all equal to $\dim K^0$. Since $J$ and $K^0$ have the same underlying space by step 6, their closed chains and dimensions agree. Therefore $\dim K_{\mathrm{red}}^\circ=\dim J=\dim K^0=\dim K$.
